Budgeting

TipHow these exercises work

Each topic starts with a real scenario and a bar model, then three levels of exercises. Level 1 (Guided) fills in the blanks of a finished function. Level 2 (Practice) applies it to new numbers. Level 3 (Challenge) asks a new question with little scaffolding. The R and Python exercises run in your browser: click Run Code to try, Submit Answer to check, and use the hint or solution if you get stuck. Excel exercises have a solution you can reveal.

Book Topics

  • Mindset shift: a budget is intentional allocation, not restriction; reframe “I have to spend” as “my needs cost”; room for error is the most underrated concept (Housel)
  • Expense categories: fixed (lock in and automate), variable (category limits, not line by line tracking), periodic (set aside 1/12 of the annual cost each month)
  • Sinking funds: $1,200/year car insurance becomes $100/month; gifts $600 → $50, car maintenance $1,200 → $100, vacation $2,400 → $200
  • Zero-based budgeting: every dollar of a $5,000 paycheck gets a job and the remainder is $0; best for anyone rebuilding from debt or with irregular income
  • Percentage-based budgeting: Sethi’s Conscious Spending Plan (fixed 50 to 60%, investments 10%+, savings 5 to 10%, guilt-free 20 to 35%) next to the 50/30/20 rule
  • Recommendation: zero-based for 2 to 3 months, then graduate to percentages with automation
  • Tools: a spreadsheet with tabs for income, fixed, variable, sinking funds, net worth, and a summary; the best tool is the one you will actually use
  • Budgeting math: percentages, annualizing and monthly-izing, opportunity cost, break-even
  • Financial Order of Operations: the budget shows how much is left over; Preston’s FOO shows where it goes next

Percentages

The foundational budgeting calculation: what share of income does each expense represent? Picture income as one bar and each expense as a slice of it.

Formula: (Expense ÷ Income) × 100

Book example: rent of $1,500 on $5,000 of take-home pay is 30% of income.

Level 1: Guided

Fill in the blanks to finish percent_of_income(), then find what share of a $5,000 paycheck goes to $1,500 of rent.

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

With the expense in B2 (1500) and income in C2 (5000), write the percentage in D2.

NoteSolution 
=(B2 / C2) * 100

This returns 30. Or enter =B2 / C2 and format the cell as a Percentage.

#| exercise: pct_1_py
def percent_of_income(expense, income):
    return (______ / ______) * 100

percent_of_income(1500, 5000)

The share is the part (the expense) divided by the whole (income).

Solution. 

def percent_of_income(expense, income):
    return (expense / income) * 100

percent_of_income(1500, 5000)
#| exercise: pct_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 30) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: rent is 30% of take-home pay."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Divide the expense by income."}
feedback
#| exercise: pct_1_r
percent_of_income <- function(expense, income) {
  (______ / ______) * 100
}
percent_of_income(1500, 5000)

The share is the part (the expense) divided by the whole (income).

Solution. 

percent_of_income <- function(expense, income) {
  (expense / income) * 100
}
percent_of_income(1500, 5000)
#| exercise: pct_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 30))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: rent is 30% of take-home pay.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Divide the expense by income.")
}

Level 2: Practice

Here is the book’s zero-based budget for a $5,000 paycheck. What percent of income goes to Investments and Savings combined?

Category Amount
Rent $1,500
Groceries $500
Transport $300
Investments $1,000
Savings $500
Fun Money $700
Other $500
  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Put categories in A2:A8, amounts in B2:B8, and income in E1. Find the combined percentage for Investments and Savings.

NoteSolution

In C2, lock the income cell with $ and fill down to C8:

=B2 / $E$1 * 100

Then add the two rows: =C5 + C6. The answer is 30.

#| exercise: pct_2_py
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
def percent_of_income(expense, income):
    return (expense / income) * 100

budget = pd.DataFrame({
    "category": ["Rent", "Groceries", "Transport", "Investments",
                 "Savings", "Fun Money", "Other"],
    "amount": [1500, 500, 300, 1000, 500, 700, 500]
})
#| exercise: pct_2_py
budget["pct"] = percent_of_income(budget["amount"], 5000)
budget.loc[budget["category"].isin(______), "pct"].sum()

isin() takes a list: ["Investments", "Savings"].

Solution. 

budget["pct"] = percent_of_income(budget["amount"], 5000)
budget.loc[budget["category"].isin(["Investments", "Savings"]), "pct"].sum()
#| exercise: pct_2_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 30) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: 30% of income goes to your future self."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Keep only Investments and Savings, then add their percentages."}
feedback
#| exercise: pct_2_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
percent_of_income <- function(expense, income) {
  (expense / income) * 100
}
budget <- data.frame(
  category = c("Rent", "Groceries", "Transport", "Investments",
               "Savings", "Fun Money", "Other"),
  amount   = c(1500, 500, 300, 1000, 500, 700, 500)
)
#| exercise: pct_2_r
budget |>
  mutate(pct = percent_of_income(amount, 5000)) |>
  filter(category %in% ______) |>
  summarise(total = sum(pct)) |>
  pull(total)

%in% takes a vector: c("Investments", "Savings").

Solution. 

budget |>
  mutate(pct = percent_of_income(amount, 5000)) |>
  filter(category %in% c("Investments", "Savings")) |>
  summarise(total = sum(pct)) |>
  pull(total)
#| exercise: pct_2_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 30))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: 30% of income goes to your future self.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Keep only Investments and Savings, then add their percentages.")
}

Level 3: Challenge

Rent goes up from $1,500 to $1,800. To keep the budget zero-based (every dollar still adds up to $5,000), you take the extra $300 out of Fun Money. What percent of income is Fun Money now?

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Change the rent amount in B2, then change B7 (Fun Money) so B9 (the total) is still 5,000.

NoteSolution

Set B2 to 1800 and B7 to =700 - (B2 - 1500), which is 400. C7 then shows 8, and C9 still reads 100.

#| exercise: pct_3_py
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
def percent_of_income(expense, income):
    return (expense / income) * 100

budget = pd.DataFrame({
    "category": ["Rent", "Groceries", "Transport", "Investments",
                 "Savings", "Fun Money", "Other"],
    "amount": [1500, 500, 300, 1000, 500, 700, 500]
})
#| exercise: pct_3_py
# raise rent, cut Fun Money by the same amount, and return Fun Money's percent

Change a single cell with budget.loc[budget["category"] == "Rent", "amount"] = 1800. Check that budget["amount"].sum() is still 5000.

Solution. 

budget.loc[budget["category"] == "Rent", "amount"] = 1800
budget.loc[budget["category"] == "Fun Money", "amount"] -= 300
fun = budget.loc[budget["category"] == "Fun Money", "amount"].sum()
percent_of_income(fun, 5000)
#| exercise: pct_3_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 8) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: Fun Money drops from 14% to 8%. Rent increases hit somewhere."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Fun Money should fall from $700 to $400."}
feedback
#| exercise: pct_3_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
percent_of_income <- function(expense, income) {
  (expense / income) * 100
}
budget <- data.frame(
  category = c("Rent", "Groceries", "Transport", "Investments",
               "Savings", "Fun Money", "Other"),
  amount   = c(1500, 500, 300, 1000, 500, 700, 500)
)
#| exercise: pct_3_r
# raise rent, cut Fun Money by the same amount, and return Fun Money's percent

Inside mutate(), use case_when() to change only the Rent and Fun Money rows, and .default = amount to keep the rest. Check that sum(amount) is still 5000.

Solution. 

budget |>
  mutate(amount = case_when(
    category == "Rent" ~ 1800,
    category == "Fun Money" ~ amount - 300,
    .default = amount
  )) |>
  filter(category == "Fun Money") |>
  mutate(pct = percent_of_income(amount, 5000)) |>
  pull(pct)
#| exercise: pct_3_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 8))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: Fun Money drops from 14% to 8%. Rent increases hit somewhere.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Fun Money should fall from $700 to $400.")
}

Annualizing and Monthly-izing

Scale any spending habit across time periods to see the true cost. Each period is the shorter one multiplied by how many times it fits.

Formula: Cost over a longer period = Cost per period × Number of periods it contains

Daily → Weekly: × 7

Weekly → Monthly: × 4.33 (not 4)

Monthly → Annual: × 12

Daily → Annual: × 365

Annual → Monthly: ÷ 12

Book example: a $5 daily coffee is $5 × 365 = $1,825 per year.

Level 1: Guided

Fill in the blanks to finish to_annual(), then find the yearly cost of a $5 daily coffee.

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Put the daily cost in A1 (5). In A2, find the yearly cost.

NoteSolution 
=A1 * 365

This returns $1,825.

#| exercise: annual_1_py
def to_annual(amount, period="daily"):
    factors = {"daily": ______, "weekly": 52, "monthly": ______}
    return amount * factors[period]

to_annual(5, "daily")

How many days are in a year? How many months?

Solution. 

def to_annual(amount, period="daily"):
    factors = {"daily": 365, "weekly": 52, "monthly": 12}
    return amount * factors[period]

to_annual(5, "daily")
#| exercise: annual_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 1825) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: $1,825 a year, about the price of a vacation."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. A year has 365 days and 12 months."}
feedback
#| exercise: annual_1_r
to_annual <- function(amount, period = "daily") {
  factors <- c(daily = ______, weekly = 52, monthly = ______)
  amount * factors[[period]]
}
to_annual(5, "daily")

How many days are in a year? How many months?

Solution. 

to_annual <- function(amount, period = "daily") {
  factors <- c(daily = 365, weekly = 52, monthly = 12)
  amount * factors[[period]]
}
to_annual(5, "daily")
#| exercise: annual_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 1825))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: $1,825 a year, about the price of a vacation.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. A year has 365 days and 12 months.")
}

Level 2: Practice

The book’s sinking funds turn yearly costs into monthly set-asides: car insurance $1,200, gifts $600, car maintenance $1,200, and a vacation $2,400. How much do you need to set aside each month for all four?

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Put the names in A2:A5 and yearly costs in B2:B5. Find each monthly amount in column C and the total in C6.

NoteSolution

In C2, then fill down:

=B2 / 12

Then =SUM(C2:C5) returns $450.

#| exercise: annual_2_py
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
sinking = pd.DataFrame({
    "expense": ["Car insurance", "Christmas/gifts", "Car maintenance", "Annual vacation"],
    "annual": [1200, 600, 1200, 2400]
})
#| exercise: annual_2_py
sinking["monthly"] = ______
sinking["monthly"].sum()

Divide the whole annual column by 12.

Solution. 

sinking["monthly"] = sinking["annual"] / 12
sinking["monthly"].sum()
#| exercise: annual_2_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 450) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: $450 a month means none of these bills is ever a surprise."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Divide each yearly cost by 12, then add them up."}
feedback
#| exercise: annual_2_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
sinking <- data.frame(
  expense = c("Car insurance", "Christmas/gifts", "Car maintenance", "Annual vacation"),
  annual  = c(1200, 600, 1200, 2400)
)
#| exercise: annual_2_r
sinking |>
  mutate(monthly = ______) |>
  summarise(total = sum(monthly)) |>
  pull(total)

Divide the annual column by 12.

Solution. 

sinking |>
  mutate(monthly = annual / 12) |>
  summarise(total = sum(monthly)) |>
  pull(total)
#| exercise: annual_2_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 450))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: $450 a month means none of these bills is ever a surprise.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Divide each yearly cost by 12, then add them up.")
}

Level 3: Challenge

Three habits are paid on different schedules: coffee $5 a day, groceries $150 a week, and streaming $15.99 a month. What do they cost together in a year?

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Put habits in A2:A4, amounts in B2:B4, and periods (“daily”, “weekly”, “monthly”) in C2:C4. Find each yearly cost in D and the total.

NoteSolution

In D2, then fill down:

=B2 * SWITCH(C2, "daily", 365, "weekly", 52, "monthly", 12)

Then =SUM(D2:D4) returns $9,816.88.

#| exercise: annual_3_py
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
def to_annual(amount, period="daily"):
    factors = {"daily": 365, "weekly": 52, "monthly": 12}
    return amount * factors[period]

habits = pd.DataFrame({
    "habit": ["Coffee", "Groceries", "Streaming"],
    "amount": [5, 150, 15.99],
    "period": ["daily", "weekly", "monthly"]
})
#| exercise: annual_3_py
# find each habit's yearly cost, then the total

to_annual() takes one row at a time. Use habits.apply(lambda row: to_annual(row["amount"], row["period"]), axis=1).

Solution. 

habits["annual"] = habits.apply(lambda row: to_annual(row["amount"], row["period"]), axis=1)
habits["annual"].sum()
#| exercise: annual_3_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 9816.88) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: $9,816.88 a year. Groceries are most of it."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Each habit needs its own period's factor."}
feedback
#| exercise: annual_3_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
to_annual <- function(amount, period = "daily") {
  factors <- c(daily = 365, weekly = 52, monthly = 12)
  amount * factors[[period]]
}
habits <- data.frame(
  habit  = c("Coffee", "Groceries", "Streaming"),
  amount = c(5, 150, 15.99),
  period = c("daily", "weekly", "monthly")
)
#| exercise: annual_3_r
# find each habit's yearly cost, then the total

to_annual() takes one period at a time. Inside mutate(), use mapply(to_annual, amount, period) to run it on each row.

Solution. 

habits |>
  mutate(annual = mapply(to_annual, amount, period)) |>
  summarise(total = sum(annual)) |>
  pull(total)
#| exercise: annual_3_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 9816.88))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: $9,816.88 a year. Groceries are most of it.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Each habit needs its own period's factor.")
}

Opportunity Cost

Every dollar spent is also what that dollar could have become. The hidden cost of any purchase is its future value if invested instead.

Formula: amount × (1 + r)^n

Book example: choosing a $15,000 used car over a $40,000 new one and investing the $25,000 difference at 7% for 30 years gives $25,000 × (1.07)^30 ≈ $190,000.

Level 1: Guided

Fill in the blanks to finish opportunity_cost(), then find what the $25,000 saved on a used car grows to in 30 years at 7%.

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Put the amount in A2 (25000), the rate in B2 (0.07), and years in C2 (30). Find the future value in D2.

NoteSolution 
=A2*(1+B2)^C2

This returns $190,306.38.

#| exercise: opp_1_py
def opportunity_cost(amount, rate, years):
    return amount * (1 + ______) ** ______

opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, 30)

Grow by (1 + rate) once for every year.

Solution. 

def opportunity_cost(amount, rate, years):
    return amount * (1 + rate) ** years

opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, 30)
#| exercise: opp_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 190306.38) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: about $190,000. That's the real price of the new car."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Raise (1 + rate) to the number of years."}
feedback
#| exercise: opp_1_r
opportunity_cost <- function(amount, rate, years) {
  amount * (1 + ______)^______
}
opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, 30)

Grow by (1 + rate) once for every year.

Solution. 

opportunity_cost <- function(amount, rate, years) {
  amount * (1 + rate)^years
}
opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, 30)
#| exercise: opp_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 190306.38, tolerance = 1e-6))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: about $190,000. That's the real price of the new car.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Raise (1 + rate) to the number of years.")
}

Level 3: Challenge

At 7%, how many whole years does it take for the $25,000 to double to $50,000?

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Put years 1 to 20 in A5:A24, find the value at each year in B, then find the first year at or above $50,000.

NoteSolution

In B5, then fill down:

=$A$2*(1+$B$2)^A5

Then =MATCH(TRUE, B5:B24>=50000, 0) returns 11. You can also solve it directly with =ROUNDUP(NPER(7%, 0, -25000, 50000), 0).

#| exercise: opp_3_py
#| setup: true
def opportunity_cost(amount, rate, years):
    return amount * (1 + rate) ** years
#| exercise: opp_3_py
years = 1
# keep adding a year until the value reaches $50,000

years

Use while opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, years) < 50000: and add 1 to years inside the loop.

Solution. 

years = 1
while opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, years) < 50000:
    years += 1

years
#| exercise: opp_3_py
#| check: true
if result == 11:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: 11 years. The rule of 72 (72 / 7 = about 10.3) gets you close."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Stop at the first year the value is at least $50,000."}
feedback
#| exercise: opp_3_r
#| setup: true
opportunity_cost <- function(amount, rate, years) {
  amount * (1 + rate)^years
}
#| exercise: opp_3_r
years <- 1:20
# find the first year the value is at least $50,000

opportunity_cost() is vectorized, so pass all 20 years at once. Then use min(years[...]).

Solution. 

years <- 1:20
value <- opportunity_cost(25000, 0.07, years)
min(years[value >= 50000])
#| exercise: opp_3_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 11))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: 11 years. The rule of 72 (72 / 7 = about 10.3) gets you close.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Stop at the first year the value is at least $50,000.")
}

Break-Even

Useful for evaluating memberships, subscriptions, refinances, or any purchase with an upfront cost and recurring savings. Break-even is the first month cumulative savings meets the upfront cost.

Formula: Upfront Cost ÷ Monthly Savings = months to break even

Book example: a $500 membership that saves $60/month breaks even in $500 ÷ $60 = 8.3 months.

Level 1: Guided

Fill in the blanks to finish months_to_break_even(), then find how long a $500 membership that saves $60 a month takes to pay for itself.

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

With the upfront cost in A2 (500) and monthly savings in B2 (60), find the months in C2.

NoteSolution 
=A2 / B2

This returns 8.33 months.

#| exercise: be_1_py
def months_to_break_even(upfront_cost, monthly_savings):
    return ______ / ______

months_to_break_even(500, 60)

How many months of savings does it take to cover the upfront cost?

Solution. 

def months_to_break_even(upfront_cost, monthly_savings):
    return upfront_cost / monthly_savings

months_to_break_even(500, 60)
#| exercise: be_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 500 / 60) < 0.001:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: about 8.3 months."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Divide the upfront cost by the monthly savings."}
feedback
#| exercise: be_1_r
months_to_break_even <- function(upfront_cost, monthly_savings) {
  ______ / ______
}
months_to_break_even(500, 60)

How many months of savings does it take to cover the upfront cost?

Solution. 

months_to_break_even <- function(upfront_cost, monthly_savings) {
  upfront_cost / monthly_savings
}
months_to_break_even(500, 60)
#| exercise: be_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 500 / 60))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: about 8.3 months.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Divide the upfront cost by the monthly savings.")
}

Level 2: Practice

Refinancing a loan costs $3,000 upfront and lowers your payment by $110 a month. Savings arrive in whole months, so in which month do you break even?

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Put 3000 in A2 and 110 in B2. Round up to a whole month.

NoteSolution 
=ROUNDUP(A2 / B2, 0)

This returns 28. If you plan to sell the house sooner than that, the refinance doesn’t pay.

#| exercise: be_2_py
#| setup: true
import math
def months_to_break_even(upfront_cost, monthly_savings):
    return upfront_cost / monthly_savings

Check if monthly_savings <= 0: first and return math.inf. Otherwise return the division.

Solution. 

import math
def safe_break_even(upfront_cost, monthly_savings):
    if monthly_savings <= 0:
        return math.inf
    return upfront_cost / monthly_savings

Check if (monthly_savings <= 0) first and return(Inf). Otherwise return the division.

Solution. 

safe_break_even <- function(upfront_cost, monthly_savings) {
  if (monthly_savings <= 0) {
    return(Inf)
  }
  upfront_cost / monthly_savings
}
c(safe_break_even(500, 0), safe_break_even(500, -10), safe_break_even(500, 60))
#| exercise: be_3_r
#| check: true

  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: no savings means it never pays for itself.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Zero and negative savings should both return Inf.")
}
